scope: Focused anchor-gate review of three Africa/Middle East rural systems. The review searched for a mappable 1100-1500 boundary, a defensible two-sided people/capacity interval, local-food support and independent pressure evidence. No record passes the two-sided training-anchor standard; all are retained as explicit validation or rejection packets rather than being converted into synthetic targets.

promotion_audit.decision: No new training target is admitted. Fayyum has unusually rich village, crop, water and fiscal evidence but the accessible record does not expose a complete total-population interval or an independently demonstrated saturation fraction. Tulkarm has local-food and pressure language plus later Ottoman household counts, but the numerical count is from 1535 rather than the 1354 waqf boundary. Hubras/Saham has archaeological evidence of late-fourteenth-century agricultural and settlement pressure but no population interval. None satisfies the two-sided aggregate-anchor gate.
promotion_audit.review_method: Each source was checked for date and technology compatibility, population semantics, local-food dependence, independent pressure/saturation evidence, shock and trade confounding, historical-boundary definition, source-family independence and EU5 crosswalk closure. Population numbers are not inferred from poll tax, households, taxes, settlement size or density language.

records.label: Fayyum al-Nabulusi 1245 village survey - anchor gate review
records.interval_semantics: Rejected as a two-sided target pending direct access to the population tables behind Rapoport's Chapter 3 reconstruction. The 1245 al-Nabulusi material is a detailed fiscal/agricultural village survey, not a complete population census. Poll-tax heads are partial taxable non-Muslim/adult counts and cannot be multiplied into total inhabitants or treated as a lower bound on all residents.
quantitative_evidence: Keenan, 'Fayyum Agriculture at the End of the Ayyubid Period' (Proceedings of the British Academy 96, 1999), PDF pp. 287-292, describes al-Nabulusi's Chapter 10 gazetteer of about 100 taxed villages and the village as the basic unit of economic reproduction, administration and taxation.

Keenan 1999, PDF pp. 292-294, records village size qualifiers, hamlets/out-villages, canal and water-right allocations and crop assessments; pp. 297-298 give the Talit example with wheat, barley and sesame crop quantities and an explicit statement that it was a small village in population.

Rapoport and Shahar, 'Rural Society in Medieval Islam' project abstract (QMUL/IAST, 2021), pp. 4-5, states that the 1245 audit covers more than 100 villages and records location, size, tribe, religious composition, water source, fiscal revenue, crop taxes, seed advances, poll tax and sugar; most village locations can be reconstructed for GIS.

The QMUL Minyat al-Usquf translation (entry for the 1245 register) records a small irrigated village with orchards and 56 poll-tax individuals (47 resident and 9 absent). The entry is a partial tax category, not a total population interval: https://projects.history.qmul.ac.uk/ruralsocietyislam/translations/minyat-al-usquf/.

Rapoport, Rural Economy and Tribal Society in Islamic Egypt (2018), Chapter 3, is cited by the EH.Net review as estimating cultivated land and local population from al-Nabulusi, but the exact population table/interval is not openly available in the reviewed sources: https://eh.net/book_reviews/rural-economy-and-tribal-society-in-islamic-egypt-a-study-of-al-nabulusis-villages-of-the-fayyum/.

The Sehepunkte review of Rapoport (2021) describes the 1245 fiscal survey, map and downloadable Excel database, and explicitly notes that it is not a complete reconstruction because untaxed activities are invisible: https://www.sehepunkte.de/2021/02/druckfassung/35574.html.
pressure_evidence: Keenan 1999, PDF pp. 288-289, discusses abandonment/desertion and resettlement in the Fayyum during the eleventh-century price and water crisis; this is historical pressure context, not a 1245 saturation interval.

The source records irrigation quotas, canal maintenance and crop levies, so it supplies local production-pressure features. It does not independently establish what fraction of long-run local carrying capacity was occupied in 1245.
shock_flags: partial poll tax excludes Muslims and non-taxable demographic groups
fiscal levies are assessments, not net edible calories
village/grid map is not yet a closed 124-village aggregate polygon
Cairo/Nile redistribution and trade dependence are not quantified
exact population reconstruction cited by Rapoport is not available for audit
records.trade_dependence: Local Nile agriculture is documented, including cereals, legumes, rice, sugar, gardens and livestock, but the net import/export share of the surveyed villages is unresolved.
records.food_regime: Nile irrigation, cereals, legumes, rice, sugar cane, livestock and village orchards/gardens
records.boundary_description: The more-than-100 (and project database 124-row) villages and hamlets in al-Nabulusi's Fayyum survey, linked by canal and water-right entries. The QMUL map and database identify points/grid cells but do not provide a fully audited aggregate polygon equivalent to an EU5 province.
records.boundary_source: Queen Mary Rural Society in Medieval Islam database and Fayyum map; Keenan 1999, pp. 287-298
records.boundary_confidence: medium for named village/grid points; low for complete historical aggregate
records.source_family_independence: Independent primary-register/database and historical study family; the same broad Fayyum source family as the existing fiscal holdout, so it adds no independent population scale anchor.
missing_criteria: auditable two-sided population interval for the same 124-village boundary
literature-supported saturation fraction or capacity interval independent of the fiscal source
complete historical polygon and >=95% EU5 area crosswalk
direct page/table extraction of Rapoport Chapter 3 estimates
records.notes: This packet is intentionally strict: the rich Fayyum records should improve physical feature lineage and become a target only after the population table and boundary are directly audited. No poll-tax, village-size adjective or crop levy is converted into people.

records.label: Tulkarm waqf village - 1354 boundary with 1535 household count
records.interval_semantics: Rejected as a 1354 two-sided target because the numerical population evidence belongs to a later Ottoman defter. The article describes a 1354 waqf order assigning two-thirds of Tulkarm's agricultural land, but its 95-household/approximately-522-person figure is explicitly from the 940H/1535 Ottoman Defterler-i Mufassal; 1548 gives 189 households/approximately 1,040 people. Those later counts cannot label the 1354 boundary without a demonstrated demographic bridge.
quantitative_evidence: Palestine Studies, 'Tulkarm: A Palestinian Village in the Late Ottoman Period,' discussion of the 1354 waqf order and later population: the waqf assigned two-thirds of Tulkarm's agricultural land; the 1535 defter records 95 households and an estimate of 522 people using 5.5 people per household; 1548 records 189 households and about 1,040 people: https://www.palestine-studies.org/ar/node/78442, article pp. 70-82 and 139-144.

The same article's endnote 33 identifies the household/522-person source as Defterler-i Mufassal, Sham Sharif, 940H/1535 AD (Palestine Studies article endnotes, pp. 260-263). This is the decisive date mismatch.

The article describes Tulkarm as a waqf village on Wadi al-Sha'ir in the foothills/coastal plain and reports difficult long-distance communications and local self-sufficiency, but it does not give a total 1354 population or a complete rural boundary polygon.
pressure_evidence: Palestine Studies, pp. 84-99 and 191-194, characterizes Tulkarm as densely populated relative to available resources, agriculturally productive and largely self-sufficient; the statements are qualitative and are not an independent 1354 saturation interval.
The waqf land allocation and later grain-tax figures are evidence of land/resource administration, not proof that the 1354 settlement was at a long-run Malthusian equilibrium.
shock_flags: later Ottoman household-to-person multiplier is model-dependent
waqf land allocation and grain taxes do not enumerate all residents
village/hamula boundary is not an audited EU5 polygon
later Ottoman security, migration and administrative changes may alter the comparison
records.trade_dependence: The article reports self-sufficiency and difficult long-distance communication, supporting local-food relevance qualitatively; no quantitative local-food share is available.
records.food_regime: Foothill/coastal-plain grain agriculture, orchards and mixed village farming
records.boundary_description: The historic Tulkarm waqf village on Wadi al-Sha'ir and its agricultural lands. The 1354 waqf boundary is described textually but not supplied as a georeferenced polygon in the reviewed source.
records.boundary_source: Palestine Studies article, pp. 70-82, 139-144 and endnotes pp. 260-263
records.source_family_independence: Independent village-history/defter family, but the population observations are later than the 1354 land boundary and are not a 1337-compatible target.
missing_criteria: 1354 population interval for the same boundary
demographic bridge from 1354 to 1535 and shock audit
georeferenced waqf boundary and >=95% EU5 crosswalk
records.notes: The 1535 and 1548 household counts remain useful out-of-date validation evidence only. Do not back-cast 522 people to 1354 or use the article's qualitative density language as a target.

records.label: Northern Jordan Hubras and Saham villages - late Mamluk agricultural-pressure validation
records.interval_semantics: Validation-only archaeological and environmental case. The Northern Jordan Survey treats village plus agricultural/pastoral hinterland as the unit and documents late-fourteenth-century settlement/agricultural productivity reduction, but the reviewed report provides no defensible people interval, household count or saturation fraction for Hubras or Saham.
quantitative_evidence: Walker, 'The Northern Jordan Survey 2003 - Agriculture in Late Islamic Malka and Hubras Villages,' BASOR 339 (2005), DOI 10.1086/BASOR25066903, abstract: surface survey, architecture, agricultural installations and pollen were used to study Mamluk/Ottoman settlement; some reduction in settlement and agricultural productivity occurred in the late fourteenth century, but not a complete rural-decline scale estimate: https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/abs/10.1086/BASOR25066903.

Department of Antiquities of Jordan, Annual of the Department of Antiquities of Jordan 51 (2007), 'The Northern Jordan Survey 2003 - Agriculture in Late Islamic Malka and Hubras Villages,' pp. 429-470, describes the multidisciplinary village/hinterland, agricultural installations, pollen/environment and settlement fluctuations. The scanned report contains no auditable population interval: https://publication.doa.gov.jo/uploads/publications/68/ADAJ_2007_51-429-470.pdf.
pressure_evidence: The survey's late-fourteenth-century reduction in settlement and agricultural productivity is an independent environmental/archaeological pressure signal, but it does not establish a Malthusian equilibrium or the fraction of capacity occupied before the reduction.
The village-plus-hinterland framing and agricultural/pastoral market evidence are useful for local-food and land-use feature validation; no total food balance is published.
shock_flags: archaeological survey documents change but not population magnitude
late-fourteenth-century decline may include political, market and environmental causes
village and agricultural-hinterland boundary is not a closed polygon
EU5 location selectors are candidate names pending map crosswalk
records.trade_dependence: Local agricultural and pastoral production is documented, with village-market activity; the local-food share and external supply are unresolved.
records.food_regime: Northern Jordan rain-fed/seasonal agriculture, pastoralism and village-market production
records.boundary_description: Archaeological villages of Hubras and Saham with their surveyed agricultural/pastoral hinterlands in northern Jordan. The report's survey polygons and site extents have not yet been digitized into EU5 geometry.
records.source_family_independence: Independent archaeological/environmental survey family; no population label is available and the evidence cannot set the global scale.
missing_criteria: population or capacity interval for either village and the same hinterland
closed historical survey boundary and >=95% EU5 crosswalk
quantified local-food share and trade dependence
separation of environmental decline from political/market shocks
records.notes: Use as a pressure/land-use validation case after mapping the archaeological survey extents. Do not create a people target from settlement decline or infer capacity from modern village locations.
